chemicals.concentration_notes: Xylitol is exquisitely toxic to dogs at doses as low as 0.1 grams per kilogram of body weight. Cats are not affected the same way: in an experimental study, cats were given doses up to 1,000 mg/kg (1 gram per kilogram) without suffering toxic effects or significant biochemical changes. Authorities such as the ASPCA and VCA state that cats are not negatively affected by xylitol.
chemicals.description: In dogs, xylitol triggers a massive, rapid surge of insulin, causing severe hypoglycemia and sometimes acute liver failure. In cats this does not occur — cats lack the strong insulin response, and high oral doses produced no significant change in blood glucose or liver values. Xylitol is therefore not considered toxic to cats.
chemicals.name: Xylitol (Artificial Sweetener) — not toxic to cats

chemicals.concentration_notes: Tartaric acid concentration varies by grape variety. While whole grapes and raisins are dangerous, commercial processing of grape products (juice, wine, and jam/jelly) removes or thermally decomposes most of the tartrates, which is likely why processed grape products have not been associated with poisoning.
chemicals.description: Tartaric acid is the toxic principle in whole grapes and raisins that can cause acute kidney injury. It is concentrated in fresh grapes, raisins, and currants — not in processed grape jelly, where most of it is removed during manufacturing. The risk applies to whole-grape content, not to the jelly itself.
chemicals.name: Tartaric Acid / Potassium Bitartrate (in whole grapes and raisins, largely removed from jelly)

description:
Jelly and jam are not appropriate cat food, but they are generally not acutely toxic to cats. Jelly is high in sugar, and cats are obligate carnivores not built to handle it, so the most common reaction is stomach upset.

Unlike in dogs, xylitol (the sweetener in many sugar-free products) does not appear to be toxic to cats — studies and poison-control authorities report cats are not affected by it. Processed grape products such as grape jelly, juice, and wine have not been linked to poisoning, likely because processing removes most of the tartaric acid that makes whole grapes and raisins dangerous. As a precaution, however, whole grapes, raisins, and currants should still be kept away from cats.

If your cat eats jelly or jam, watch for vomiting or loose stools. Call a veterinarian or pet poison helpline if your cat ate jelly containing whole grapes, raisins, or currants, if it ate a large amount, or if you are not sure what was in it.
emergencyNote: Jelly is generally not acutely toxic to cats. Seek prompt veterinary advice mainly if the jelly contained whole grapes, raisins, or currants, or if a large amount was eaten.
name: Jelly
safetyNotes: Regular sugary jelly: not acutely toxic but very high in sugar — avoid; it is not appropriate food for cats and can cause stomach upset
Sugar-free (xylitol) jelly: xylitol is not toxic to cats (unlike dogs); the false hypoglycaemia/liver-failure alarm does not apply to cats
Processed grape jelly: not associated with poisoning — processing removes most of the tartaric acid that makes whole grapes toxic
Whole grapes, raisins, and currants: keep away from cats as a precaution; their tartaric acid can cause kidney injury and no safe dose is established
Contact your vet if your cat eats jelly made with whole grapes, raisins, or currants, or if it eats a large amount

symptoms.name: Vomiting or loose stools from sugary jelly (most common reaction)
Gastrointestinal Upset (From High Sugar/Carbohydrates)
symptoms.notes: Cats are obligate carnivores and their digestive systems are not designed to process high amounts of sugar or human foods. Consuming standard sugary jelly can easily cause general stomach upset, vomiting, and loose stools.

symptoms.name: Transient Salivation (From Xylitol in Sugar-Free Jelly)
symptoms.notes: Xylitol is a highly toxic artificial sweetener used in many sugar-free products. While it causes severe poisoning in dogs, cats appear to be naturally resistant to xylitol toxicity.

symptoms.name: Hypoglycemia / liver effects from xylitol — does NOT apply to cats (a dog risk only)
symptoms.notes: In dogs, xylitol tricks the pancreas into releasing a massive surge of insulin, driving down blood sugar and destroying the liver511. Cats lack this specific receptor-mediated pathway and do not typically suffer this reaction.
symptoms.onset: 15 to 30 minutes for a drop in blood sugar (though it can be delayed if the product digests slowly);

symptoms.name: Acute kidney injury from whole grapes, raisins, or currants (precaution; not from processed grape jelly)
symptoms.notes: Grapes contain tartaric acid, a nephrotoxin that accumulates in the kidneys of dogs and cats, causing severe cellular necrosis and acute kidney injury1516.
symptoms.onset: Vomiting usually occurs within 6 to 12 hours of ingestion;

toxicParts: Whole grape, raisin, or currant content (if present)

treatments.name: Because the toxicity of jelly depends heavily on its ingredients—most notably if it is made from grapes (which contain the nephrotoxin tartaric acid) or sweetened with xylitol

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the jelly was ingested very recently, the veterinarian will administer a specific medication (such as the α 2 ​ -adrenergic agonist dexmedetomidine) to induce vomiting and empty the stomach.
treatments.name: Early Gastrointestinal Decontamination
treatments.notes: Decontamination is highly time-sensitive and must be done before the toxins are absorbed. While activated charcoal is utilized for grape toxicosis, it is not recommended if the jelly was sugar-free, as charcoal does not effectively bind to xylitol.

treatments.description: of the procedure: The cat is hospitalized and placed on continuous IV fluids for a minimum of 48 hours36. This aggressive fluid diuresis is designed to stimulate urine production and protect the kidneys, while the veterinary team closely monitors the cat's renal function (e.g., serum creatinine) and fluid balance.
treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluid Diuresis (For Grape Jelly)
treatments.notes: This treatment is implemented to prevent anuric renal failure (acute kidney injury), which is associated with the tartaric acid found in grapes and raisins.

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the cat ingested sugar-free jelly containing xylitol, they may be admitted for monitoring. If the cat's blood sugar begins to drop, the veterinarian will administer IV fluids containing sugar (dextrose) to stabilize blood glucose levels, potentially alongside liver protectants to manage any hepatic injury411.
treatments.name: Hypoglycemia and Liver Management (For Sugar-Free Jelly)
treatments.notes: While xylitol is a deadly toxin to dogs (causing a massive insulin surge, severe hypoglycemia, and liver failure), cats appear to be naturally resistant to xylitol1213.

treatments.description: of the procedure: If the cat consumes standard, safe-fruit jelly (like strawberry or apple), the primary issue is a carbohydrate/sugar overload. The veterinarian will treat resulting tummy upset with anti-nausea medications and recommend a temporary bland diet while the digestive tract recovers1617.
treatments.name: Symptomatic Care for Gastrointestinal Upset (For Sugary Jelly)
treatments.notes: Cats are obligate carnivores and cannot properly process high amounts of dietary sugar1819. This results in mild to moderate gastrointestinal irritation, vomiting, and diarrhea, which typically resolves quickly with basic supportive care.
